extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of comedy/theatre/film
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for recognizing the conventions of farce as a comedy genre and for creating farcical works (stage or film). Emphasizes characteristic devices such as exaggerated situations, physical humor, stylized performance, narrative constraints, and typical form/setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on exaggerated, improbable, or ridiculous situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce is a form of comedy that relies on exaggerated, improbable, or ridiculous situations to entertain an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central defining device of farce; plots and set-pieces should push situations beyond the plausible to generate comic effect. Such situations are the primary engine of humor in farce, distinguishing it from comedy grounded in realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: It is typically marked by physical humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of bodily action, slapstick, visual gags, and stage/business is characteristic. Physical comedy often complements improbable situations and is especially prominent in stage and film farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce is typically marked by absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of the absurd—illogical sequence, extreme incongruity, or surreal events—are acceptable so long as they serve comedic escalation; however, farce generally preserves a degree of narrative continuity (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire, tongue-in-cheek humor, or parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce may employ satire, tongue-in-cheek humor or parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farce can mock social conventions, genres, or specific works (e.g., spoof films). The page cites Spaceballs as an example of a spoof film that functions as a farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbable scenarios and misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce commonly uses improbable scenarios and misunderstandings as comedic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots often hinge on escalating misunderstandings, mistaken identities, crossed communications, and other contrivances that compound the comic situation; these devices should be used to increase momentum and complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadly stylized characters and performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce features broadly stylized characters and performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters are frequently exaggerated stereotypes or caricatures rather than nuanced psychological portraits; performances are intentionally broad to match the heightened, ludicrous situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintains slight realism and narrative continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite involving absurd situations and characters, the genre generally maintains at least a slight degree of realism and narrative continuity within the context of the irrational or ludicrous situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This degree of causal continuity distinguishes farce from completely absurdist or fantastical genres; even extravagant action should feel coherent within the play's established logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Often episodic or short in duration; single-location settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Farces are often episodic or short in duration, often being set in one specific location where all events occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural economy is common—one-act pieces or short films staged in a single primary setting—facilitating tight timing, rapid entrances/exits, and concentrated comic escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical performance media: stage and film
rubrics_metrics.description: Farces have historically been performed for the stage and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating farce, consider staging and cinematic conventions—timing, physical business, and sight-gags—that differ by medium; historical context (medieval/Renaissance short pieces) informs traditional forms like one-act farce.
